summary: Rebecca urges Jacob not to marry among Canaanite households as Esau has done, and Jacob tells her he intends to seek a wife among her relatives. She thanks God for him and blesses his future descendants, land, peace, and a sanctuary associated with his line.
whyItMatters: The chapter turns the family distinction into a mother-son conversation and blessing before the next conflict over Isaac's blessing.

context.author: Within the book, the angel of the presence dictates the account to Moses; the historical writer is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through Moses in the book’s frame; the specific first historical audience is not identified.
context.date: The narrative places the revelation at Sinai; the historical Hebrew work is usually dated to the second century BCE, without an established exact year.
context.setting: Rebecca and Jacob speaking within Isaac's family after Esau's marriages.
context.literaryForm: Family dialogue followed by a long maternal blessing poem.

before.text: Isaac has lived amid famine and water disputes, while Esau has already given Jacob his birthright.

here.text: Rebecca and Jacob discuss marriage within their kin, and she blesses his future family and sanctuary.

after.text: Isaac asks Esau for food before blessing him, but Rebecca hears and directs Jacob to prepare food first.

outline.heading: Rebecca warns Jacob about marriage
outline.note: She contrasts her hopes for Jacob with Esau’s Canaanite wives.

outline.heading: Jacob states his intention and resolve
outline.note: He recalls Abraham’s instruction and his refusal of Esau’s suggestion.

outline.heading: Rebecca gives thanks and asks to bless
outline.note: She praises God and places her hands on Jacob.

outline.heading: The blessing over descendants and land
outline.note: Rebecca prays for righteousness, many children, and possession.

outline.heading: Sanctuary, lasting name, and farewell
outline.note: The blessing closes with divine dwelling and a maternal kiss.

keyVerses.text: For I remember, mother, the words of Abraham, our father, for he commanded me not to take a wife of the daughters of Canaan, but to take me a wife from the seed of my father's house and from my kindred.
keyVerses.why: Jacob grounds his intended marriage choice in Abraham's earlier instruction, not only Rebecca's new appeal.

keyVerses.text: And may thy name and thy seed endure to all the ages, And may the Most High God be their God, And may the God of righteousness dwell with them, And by them may His sanctuary be built unto all the ages.
keyVerses.why: The blessing connects Jacob's descendants with the future building of a sanctuary.

questions.question: Why does Rebecca raise marriage now?
questions.answer: She says Esau’s Canaanite wives have grieved her and urges Jacob to marry among her father’s relatives. The request is part of this family’s effort to preserve its covenant identity, not an assessment of every person outside it.

questions.question: What does “holy seed” mean in Rebecca’s prayer?
questions.answer: It refers to the descendants she hopes Jacob will have as a people set apart for God. The phrase is about the family’s imagined covenant future, not a biological claim that other humans are worth less.

questions.question: Does the passage endorse contempt for Canaanite people today?
questions.answer: The dialogue uses strong inherited boundaries and harsh judgments about Esau’s wives and Canaanite marriage. Those are claims within the ancient narrative; they do not justify prejudice, exclusion, or harm toward living people.

questions.question: What does Jacob tell Rebecca about his own plans?
questions.answer: He says he has not married, recalls Abraham’s instruction, and has already considered the daughters of Laban, Rebecca’s brother. He also says he has refused Esau’s repeated proposal to marry a sister of Esau’s wives.

questions.question: How does Rebecca begin the blessing?
questions.answer: She first thanks God, asks that a righteous blessing be put in her mouth, and then places her hands on Jacob’s head. The speech is presented as prayerful and deliberate, not an offhand expression of preference.

questions.question: Have the promised land possession and sanctuary building already been fulfilled?
questions.answer: No. She asks that Jacob’s descendants receive the land and that a sanctuary be built through them. Those are hopes within a blessing, not completed events in the chapter.

questions.question: How does the chapter close?
questions.answer: Rebecca ends with a prayer that God love Jacob and then kisses him. This intimate ending follows a lengthy blessing about descendants and land and precedes the next chapter’s family conflict.

glossary.def: Rebecca’s brother, whose daughters Jacob says he has considered as possible wives.
A holy dwelling for God that Rebecca asks might be built through Jacob’s descendants.
